claims.text: The target material is an as-solidified, Co-free equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy.
Dynamic deformation in as-solidified equiatomic FeNiCrMn is governed primarily by competition between dislocation slip activation and temperature-dependent defect healing or recovery.
The relevant defect-healing rate has an Arrhenius-type temperature dependence.
When imposed strain rate overwhelms defect healing, localized slip avalanches produce serrated or jerky plastic flow.
When healing is relatively effective, deformation becomes smoother and more continuous.
Identical solidification processing preserves the alloy's balanced strength-ductility microstructure.
Temperature and strain rate can be independently varied in controlled mechanical tests to test the proposed mechanism.
The proposed study covers tensile or compressive loading from quasi-static to high-rate conditions and from room temperature to elevated temperatures below melting.
Local dislocation arrangements and the density of weak slip zones are structural mediators of the dynamic response.
The onset of dynamic recrystallization or adiabatic shear-band formation is a structural mediator of the dynamic response.
The ratio of mechanical strain rate to defect-healing rate determines the dynamic response.
High strain rates or lower temperatures will produce more pronounced serrated flow through abrupt dislocation avalanches.
Lower strain rates or higher temperatures will produce smoother flow and reduced yield serration.
As-cast FeNiCrMn has a known strength-ductility balance under quasi-static room-temperature loading.
The baseline as-cast FeNiCrMn microstructure is uniform and free of significant dynamic banding.
The proposed mechanism is applicable only to the as-solidified state without prior extensive annealing or pre-straining that changes intrinsic defect structures.
High-resolution stress-strain measurements and post-deformation TEM or SEM can quantify serrations, dislocation structures, recrystallized regions, and shear bands.

The hypothesis would be falsified by absence of a systematic temperature/strain-rate correlation with the smooth-to-serrated transition, or by a different mechanism dominating independently of the proposed competition.
